title.narrative: Advancing Transformative Agricultural Systems in Grenada through the Promotion of Integrated and Resilient Ecosystem approaches throughout the cocoa value chain (ASPIRE)

description.narrative: Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

Overarching Benefits. The ASPIRE Project aims to enhance the sustainability of Grenada's food system by fostering resilience among farmers and ecosystems through integrated cocoa agroforestry landscape approaches. This initiative promotes a diversified, competitive, and climate-resilient cocoa value chain, benefiting 8,000 individuals, including 40% women. By improving the management of 1,000 hectares, restoring 574 hectares, and sequestering -158,486 tCO2-eq. over 20 years, the project drives transformative change, addressing climate risks and advancing sustainable agricultural practices. The Economic and Financial Analysis (EFA) to assess its contribution to Project beneficiaries and society. The aim of the EFA is to compare the costs and benefits of the Project and assess its viability, both from the point of view of the beneficiaries (financial analysis) and from that of the economy (economic analysis). It also follows an incremental rationale to evaluate additional benefits and costs generated by the Project, in contrast with inaction. The project’s Theory of Change (ToC) informs the EFA methodology, addressing key challenges such as climate risks, governance of resources, and institutional capacity gaps to enhance resilience and sustainability in agrifood systems. The EFA focuses on the quantitative assessment of cost and benefits from investment models, which represent the main project activities and expected results. The EFA follows an incremental assessment of the investment models, comparing the with-project (WP) situation with the without-project (WOP) situation to determine the additional benefits, while considering the additional costs. The models analyzed generate positive financial benefits for Project beneficiaries, compared to the WOP situation. The improvements from the WOP to the WP relate mainly to increased efficiency and reduced losses in the context of climate change, as well as improved conditions for access to markets and capitalization. The restoration and conservation of ecosystem services is at the base of increased and sustained productivity. Sources of benefits considered in the economic analysis. The economic analysis integrates the flows of incremental economic benefits and costs for the total number of investment models implemented by the project. In line with the ToC, the project generates other relevant economic benefits beyond those directly quantified in the investment models. The enhanced management of natural resources in strategic watersheds of the country would result in a sustainable provision of key ecosystem services. The quantitative assessment incorporates four sources of economic valuations for ecosystem services linked to project investments. I) Agritourism and Biodiversity: At least one-third of beneficiaries can leverage agroforestry landscapes for agritourism opportunities, preserving biodiversity and generating income. II) Disaster Risk Reduction: Investments mitigate damages from extreme events like hurricanes and droughts for direct and indirect beneficiaries. III) EU Regulation Compliance: The project ensures agricultural exports meet the European Union’s Deforestation-Free Products Regulation, safeguarding market access and avoiding economic losses. III) Climate Change Mitigation: Project activities result in a net reduction of 158,480 tCO2e over 20 years. The economic valuation of GHG mitigation follows World Bank methodologies, yielding higher NPVs under both low and high carbon price scenarios. Other benefits and co-benefits. Other important benefits relate to climate change adaptation at landscape level, like water regulation, erosion control, pollination, pest and disease control, are not captured at full extent in the targeted watersheds due to limited information. The project includes actions to improve the assessment and knowledge of these benefits. Other economic co-benefit at macro level, such as employment generation (direct, indirect and induced) and overall contribution to food and nutrition security, are not included in the quantitative analysis given the lack of detailed information. However, these are relevant contributions to sustainable development goals and would be considered for impact evaluation at project completion. The analysis shows that the project is an economically viable investment for society. The project is economically viable, with incremental NPVs of $14.59 million at a 6% social discount rate in the baseline scenario – without including climate change mitigation benefits – over a period of 20 years. When accounting for the projected net reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, the IRR rises to 25%, with an NPV of $24.94 million using a high carbon price. Sensitivity analyses confirm the project’s robustness, demonstrating resilience to benefit reductions (up to 22%) and cost increases (up to 28%).

To drive transformative change in the Grenadian agricultural system by creating a diversified, competitive, and climate-resilient cocoa value chain, that fosters sustainable and inclusive growth and poverty reduction in the country
